summary:
Eskişehir stands under the national framework applicable in Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes with articles criminalising behaviour "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and its "promotion", carrying up to three years' prison through an amendment to the indecent-acts provision. The same package would impose sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care, including a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility requirements, and could expose trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists to charges. The government justified the measures as protecting "the family and public morals".

Eskişehir is one of the country's few interior cities with a functioning Pride tradition, and that tradition has been suppressed by force. In June 2021 police blocked the city's first Pride parade. Duvar English reported that officers reached the assembly area hours before the scheduled start time and carried out identity checks; organisers were not permitted to hold a press meeting or conduct the march, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of violating the ban on the march. The intervention came days after police actions against Pride events in Istanbul and Ankara, and Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned Pride events in recent years on security and public-order grounds.

The legal baseline residents and visitors encounter is mixed. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised.

Pride has been banned in most years since 2015, with participants facing police attacks. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex"; that provision was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion in Turkey has moved measurably in the opposite direction to official policy. Kadir Has University surveys recorded support for equal rights for LGBTQ people rising from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020, a shift that sits alongside the tightening of official rhetoric and the drafting of the 11th Judicial Package.

Eskişehir's suppression did not occur in isolation. The police operation against its first planned Pride march followed interventions in Istanbul and Ankara within the same period, indicating coordinated national handling of Pride events rather than an isolated local decision.

The draft package's status matters for expectation-setting: as reported in October 2025 it was a leaked text under government consideration, not enacted law, while the advocacy provision floated in early 2026 was dropped from that year's reform package. Enforcement patterns documented elsewhere in Turkey have nonetheless continued against trans people during periods when comparable provisions were not yet on the statute book.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available in Turkey since 1988 and requires surgery, medical examination and court permission. Residents pursuing it are subject to that full sequence, and the pending judicial package would add further eligibility hurdles and a minimum age of 25 for gender-affirming care.

Residents have no statutory anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no access to same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Complaints of discrimination in employment, housing or services therefore have no dedicated legal instrument behind them.

Organising or participating in Pride events carries a documented risk of detention. In Eskişehir in June 2021, 20 people were detained for violating a march ban, and organisers were refused both a press gathering and the march itself. Civil-society organisations and journalists face potential charges under the draft package's provisions on promoting conduct contrary to biological sex.

Local Pride organising in Eskişehir has been constrained since 2021, in a city whose university population had previously made it one of the few interior locations hosting such an event.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package reported in October 2025 has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is unresolved in the sources assembled here; the inventory records it as a leaked draft under consideration.

The disposition of the 20 people detained at Eskişehir's first planned Pride march in June 2021, including whether charges were brought or prosecutions followed, is not sourced.

No source in this inventory documents Pride activity in Eskişehir after June 2021, so whether the event has been held, refused or abandoned in subsequent years remains unresolved.

The interaction between the draft package's care restrictions and existing Health Ministry practice on gender-related medical documentation is not addressed by these sources.
